Washington is shifting the Iran conflict from the battlefield to a coordinated economic-isolation campaign aimed at collapsing the regime, with details due today. Canada walked away from trade talks with the White House, and a new peace roadmap emerged for eastern DR Congo.
► Washington Opens an Economic Front Against Iran US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent told CNBC that Washington is preparing to 'squash' the Iranian economy and 'collapse this regime,' warning allies that 'you are either with us or against us. Why it matters: This marks a deliberate pivot from military strikes to economic warfare as the primary lever against Iran, forcing every US ally and trading partner to choose sides and raising the stakes for global energy markets while Hormuz stays closed.
► Canada Walks Away From the Table as Trade War Escalates The United States imposed 50 percent tariffs on $20 billion of Canadian products early Saturday, and Canada said it would retaliate beginning 8 September after last-ditch negotiations collapsed, AP reports. Why it matters: A decades-old free-trade relationship between the closest of allies now has no clear off-ramp, and Carney's gamble that Canadians will accept economic pain to stand up to Washington is being watched closely by other governments facing Trump's pressure tactics.
► Ukraine's Political Crisis Deepens as Sacked Minister Demands Wartime Elections Ukraine's dismissed defence minister, Mykhailo Fedorov, told the BBC that President Volodymyr Zelensky should be asked what he knew about corruption in his inner circle, pointing to a money-laundering investigation announced last week, while insistin Why it matters: A public challenge to Zelensky's wartime leadership from a popular former minister, over both corruption and the suspension of elections, tests the political cohesion of a country fighting for its survival and could reshape Western assumptions about Ukraine's stability.
► DR Congo and M23 Agree a Roadmap for Peace Talks The Democratic Republic of Congo's government and the Rwanda-backed M23 rebel group agreed a roadmap for peace talks after five days of negotiations in Switzerland, the BBC reports. Why it matters: A concrete, internationally backed roadmap with a ceasefire-monitoring mechanism is the most tangible step yet toward ending one of Africa's deadliest conflicts, with implications for regional stability and the global supply of critical minerals.
► Coordinated Arson Wave Hits Thailand's Insurgency-Hit South More than 50 coordinated arson and incendiary attacks 'aimed at creating unrest' were carried out across Thailand's southern border provinces between 20:00 and midnight on Saturday, the Thai military's Internal Security Operations Command said, per t Why it matters: A coordinated, nationwide-style escalation in Thailand's long-running southern insurgency, timed around a cabinet visit, signals a breakdown in the stalled Malaysia-facilitated peace process and a renewed security challenge for Bangkok.
► China's Property Fallout Reaches a Landmark Verdict The founder of collapsed property giant Evergrande was sentenced to life in prison, the BBC reports, marking a key moment in the fallout from a collapse that shook China's property sector and rippled through the global economy. Why it matters: The Evergrande sentencing closes a chapter on the crisis that exposed the fragility of China's property-led growth model, while the Hong Kong convictions underscore Beijing's continued tightening of political control — both signals of how the world's second-largest economy is managing its internal strains.
■ The Bottom Line The defining shift today is Washington's decision to wage economic war on Iran — a coordinated isolation campaign aimed at collapsing the regime, with details due at a press conference on 24 August and Tehran warning that supporting it would be an 'act of war...

item.title: Strategic Brief: US-Canada Trade War Escalates as Talks Collapse, Washington and Ankara Friction Grows Over Israeli Strikes in Syria
item.description:
Washington imposed 50 percent tariffs on $20 billion of Canadian goods after negotiations collapsed, deepening a rupture in the Western alliance. Separately, a US envoy says Israel struck Syria without notice and may have been baiting Turkey, exposing strain inside the anti-Iran coalition.
► US-Canada Trade War Deepens After Talks Collapse The United States and Canada fell deeper into a trade war on Saturday, with Washington imposing 50 percent tariffs on $20 billion worth of Canadian goods after negotiations broke down in Washington late Friday, according to AP. Why it matters: This is not a minor tariff dispute but a widening rupture between the two closest allies in the Western alliance, one that hits a shared border economy, raises prices on both sides, and signals that economic coercion is now being applied within the US alliance network itself.
► Iran Threatens Gulf Oil Routes as US Tightens Economic War Iran's newly installed head of the Supreme National Security Council, Mohsen Rezaei, threatened Tehran's neighbors against joining new US efforts to squeeze the economy, saying Iran would retaliate in a seismic manner and target oil-shipping routes t Why it matters: Tehran's explicit threat to hit alternative oil routes widens the conflict beyond the Strait of Hormuz, and the move toward secondary sanctions threatens to drag major Iran oil buyers, including China and India, into a direct confrontation over the terms of the war.
► Israel-Turkey Tension in Syria Strains the US-Led Coalition US ambassador to Turkiye and special envoy to Syria Tom Barrack accused Israel of carrying out military strikes in Syria this week without adequate warning, calling the attacks an unnecessary escalation and suggesting they may have been aimed at bait Why it matters: A public rift between Washington's envoy and Israel over a strike aimed, in the envoy's telling, at provoking Turkey shows the US-led coalition is not monolithic; Israel's own campaign in Syria now risks colliding with Turkish interests and with Washington's attempt to hold the anti-Iran coalition together.
► Russia Strikes Kyiv and Kryvyi Rih as Ukraine Hits Krasnodar Russian aerial strikes killed at least seven people in Ukraine on Saturday, a day after a Russian drone attack on a shopping centre in President Zelenskyy's hometown of Kryvyi Rih killed at least 16 and wounded about 130, Al Jazeera reports. Why it matters: The Kryvyi Rih attack, aimed at rescue workers in a second wave, marks a grim escalation in Russia's campaign against civilian infrastructure, while Ukraine's reach into Krasnodar shows the two-way nature of the strike war as the battlefield remains frozen along much of the front.
► Wildfires Detonate Unexploded World War Ordnance Across Europe Wildfires sweeping parts of Europe are exposing and detonating buried bombs and mines left from both World War I and World War II, AP reports, as heat and drought spread across the continent. Why it matters: As climate-driven fires grow more frequent, the live munitions buried across Europe's former battlefields add a dangerous, long-ignored layer to disaster response, turning routine fire seasons into hazardous clearance operations and stretching already-strained emergency services.
■ The Bottom Line The defining development of the day is the collapse of US-Canada talks into a 50 percent tariff war, marking the clearest economic rupture yet inside the Western alliance, while the US-led camp against Iran shows internal strain as Washington's envoy accuses Israel of provoking Turkey with strikes in Syria. Iran is widening its own threat to alternative oil routes in response to fresh US pressure, and the Russia-Ukraine drone war continues to escalate on both sides of the border. The broadest picture is one of simultaneous fragmentation, as economic, military and climate pressures erode alliances and suppl...

item.title: Strategic Brief: Iran Threatens NATO's Southeast Flank as War Nears Europe, US-Pakistan Spat Erupts Over Kashmir Visit
item.description:
Tehran warns it will strike Bulgaria's Bezmer Air Base and other European targets aiding US operations, while Washington pivots from military to economic pressure on Iran. Separately, a Trump envoy's Kashmir visit strains US-Pakistan ties.
► Iran Threatens Europe's Southeast as War Nears NATO's Flank Iran has warned it will treat any country aiding US 'aggression' as a legitimate target, with southeastern Europe now in Tehran's crosshairs. Why it matters: A strike on NATO territory would be a major escalation, forcing the alliance to decide whether Article 5 applies and testing whether the Iran war can be contained to the Middle East.
► Pezeshkian Calls for Ending War as US Shifts to Economic Pressure Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian said Friday it is time to end the months-long war with the United States 'from a position of strength,' telling doctors that 'the whole world acknowledges our victory. Why it matters: The war is nearing the six-month mark with both sides signalling a desire to de-escalate, but the US pivot to sanctions and Iran's insistence on negotiating from strength leave the path to a deal uncertain.
► US Re-Designates Hezbollah as Iranian Proxy, Sanctions Funding Network The US Treasury has changed Hezbollah's legal designation from a 'terrorist organisation' to that of an Iranian proxy, calling the Lebanon-based group 'an extension' of the IRGC's Quds Force. Why it matters: The re-designation legally reframes Hezbollah as an arm of Iran's military, broadening the legal basis for sanctions and potentially complicating any Lebanon settlement.
► Ukraine War Grinds On: Russian Social Crisis Warning, Kyiv Hits Fuel Supplies Russia's ballistic missile campaign is causing record civilian deaths in Ukrainian cities, with the UN reporting 437 civilians killed in July, the highest since May 2022. Why it matters: Both sides face mounting internal strain — Ukraine from civilian losses and recruitment violence, Russia from economic and social pressure — even as neither shows willingness to compromise.
► US-Pakistan Spat Erupts Over Trump Envoy's Kashmir Visit Pakistan's Foreign Ministry summoned the top US diplomat in Islamabad on Wednesday after US Ambassador to India Sergio Gor, who also serves as Trump's special envoy for South and Central Asia, described Indian-administered Kashmir as 'an important pa Why it matters: The episode exposes the difficulty of Washington's dual-track approach to two nuclear-armed rivals, and any perceived tilt toward India could push Pakistan further from US alignment.
► Bangladesh Holds First Contested Presidential Vote in 35 Years Bangladesh has elected Mirza Fakhrul Islam Alamgir, a ruling-party veteran, as president by parliamentary vote, filling the vacancy left by Shahabuddin's resignation. Why it matters: A contested presidential vote signals a maturing of Bangladesh's political system in a strategically located South Asian state, though economic pressures will test the new leadership's stability.
■ The Bottom Line The Iran-US war is entering a new phase: Tehran is threatening NATO's European flank even as both sides signal openness to ending the conflict, with Washington pivoting to a sanctions campaign and Iran insisting it negotiates from strength. The US re-designation of Hezbollah as an Iranian proxy widens the legal and financial front, while a Trump envoy's Kashmir remarks strain US-Pakistan ties and Bangladesh holds its first contested presidential vote in decades. The central question is whether the war can be contained to the Middle East or whether Europe's southeast becomes the next front.

item.title: Strategic Brief: Iran Weighs Strikes on US Bases in Europe as War Threatens to Leap the Mediterranean, Israel Bombs Syrian Base to Block Turkish Deployment
item.description:
Iranian sources tell the FT the IRGC has assessed US bases across Europe — including in Bulgaria — as contingency targets if the conflict widens, a move that would drag NATO territory directly into a war so far confined to the Gulf. Separately, Israel struck the Abu al-Duhur airbase in Syria to prevent a Turkish deployment, opening a new Israel-Turkey flashpoint, while Russia killed at least 13 people in a nine-hour barrage on Kyiv.
► Iran's War Plan Leaps Toward Europe Two Iranian sources told the Financial Times that the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps has assessed US military installations across Europe — including in Bulgaria — as potential targets in contingency plans should the conflict with Washington inten Why it matters: If Iran extends strikes to European bases, the US-Iran war ceases to be a Middle East conflict and becomes a direct threat to NATO territory and the transatlantic logistics network that sustains both the Gulf fight and the resupply of Ukraine. It would force European governments to choose sides in a war they have so far kept at arm's length.
► Ukraine: Nine Hours of Fire Over Kyiv Russia hit Kyiv with a nine-hour barrage of ballistic and cruise missiles plus drones overnight, killing at least 13 people — 12 in the capital across three districts and one in the wider region — and injuring dozens more, according to the mayor, reg Why it matters: The strike is among the heaviest on the Ukrainian capital in weeks and undercuts any suggestion the war is winding down. It also sharpens Kyiv's repeated demand for more Patriot air-defense systems at a moment when European stocks are already stretched thin by the Iran conflict.
► The Gulf Standoff: Sanctions, Not Bullets Direct US-Iran combat has largely paused since President Trump canceled further airstrikes on 31 July, but the economic front is hardening. Why it matters: The conflict has shifted from the battlefield to the ledger. The UAE's trade cutoff removes Iran's principal lifeline for re-exports and food at a time when sanctions are tightening, but experts caution it may do little to disrupt Iran's smuggling-based sanctions-evasion network.
► West Bank: Israeli Commanders Warn of Widespread Escalation Israeli army commanders have warned of the risk of 'widespread escalation' in the occupied West Bank amid a surge in attacks by Israeli settlers, according to Anadolu Agency. Why it matters: A widespread West Bank escalation would open a second front for Israel while it is already managing the Gaza ceasefire and the wider regional war, and it risks igniting a broader Palestinian uprising at a moment of maximum regional volatility.
► Israel Bombs Syrian Airbase, Opening a New Flashpoint With Turkey Israeli warplanes struck the Abu al-Duhur airbase near Aleppo on Tuesday, hours after a Turkish delegation left the site, in what Israel's Defense Minister Israel Katz called a warning against Turkish 'dangerous adventures' in Syria, Reuters reported Why it matters: Israel's willingness to bomb a base Ankara was helping rebuild — and Washington's public rebuke of its own ally — marks Turkey's growing footprint in Syria as a central regional flashpoint.
► Africa and Europe: Sudan's Displacement Crisis, Europe's Heat Toll More than 200,000 people have been newly displaced across Sudan's Kordofan region since late last year amid intensified fighting, according to the UN's International Organization for Migration. Why it matters: Sudan's displacement wave compounds a humanitarian emergency at the intersection of Africa's Sahel and the Red Sea, an area already destabilized by the Gulf war. Europe's record heat mortality underscores a climate-driven human cost that is increasingly a strategic and economic burden on the continent.

item.title: Strategic Brief: Trump Declares 'Economic D-Day' on Iran as UAE Halts Trade, Oil Hits Four-Week High
item.description:
Washington escalates its pressure campaign on Tehran with sweeping economic-warfare threats, and the UAE — long Iran's key sanctions-escape hub — suspends trade with the Islamic Republic. Oil prices climb to a near four-week high as the Strait of Hormuz standoff drags on with no off-ramp in sight.
► Washington's 'Economic D-Day' and the UAE Break President Donald Trump on Wednesday declared what he called an 'Economic D-Day' against Iran, promising 'Economic Warfare and Isolation on an unprecedented scale' and warning of 'tremendous economic consequences' for any country that helps Tehran, ac Why it matters: The UAE's trade halt removes one of Iran's most important sanctions-escape routes, materially tightening the economic noose Washington has been trying to close since April.
► Hormuz Standoff Grinds On as Oil Climbs Oil prices rose about 1% on Wednesday and settled near a four-week high as investors weighed escalating Middle East tensions, Reuters and CNBC report. Why it matters: With the ceasefire expired and both sides publicly ruling out talks, the market is pricing a prolonged closure risk that keeps energy prices elevated and global supply chains under strain.
► Ukraine: Civilian Drone Toll and Wartime Election Pressure Russian drone attacks killed at least five people in Ukraine's southern Kherson region, the governor said, with President Volodymyr Zelenskyy condemning what he called a 'safari' hunt against civilians, according to The Hindu and Al Arabiya. Why it matters: The civilian drone toll keeps the humanitarian cost of the war in focus, while the wartime-election debate and a corruption probe add internal political strain to Kyiv at a moment of external military pressure.
► Gaza Ceasefire Doubt Deepens After Kushner Visit Deadly Israeli airstrikes in Gaza have cast fresh doubt on ceasefire progress just days after US envoy Jared Kushner ended a trip to the region that failed to advance a deal, US News reports. Why it matters: The strikes undercut the US-brokered ceasefire track just as Washington's envoy departed, signaling the Gaza front remains a live source of escalation rather than a path to de-escalation.
► Asia-Pacific: Fears of a US Retreat as Carrier Heads West Trump's abrupt rollback of joint military exercises with South Korea is fueling growing fears of a US retreat from Asia, the Council on Foreign Relations argues, with the decision draining confidence in Washington's regional security commitments. Why it matters: With the Pacific carrier presence thinning and drills cut, the Iran war is forcing Washington to confront the strategic cost of deterring China while its naval resources are stretched thin.
■ The Bottom Line The defining development of the day is Washington's escalation of economic warfare against Iran — capped by the UAE's decision to halt trade with Tehran, stripping Iran of a key sanctions-escape route — even as the Strait of Hormuz standoff remains deadlocked with the ceasefire expired. Oil is climbing toward four-week highs on the uncertainty. Elsewhere, the picture is one of grinding pressure: Russian drone strikes keep killing civilians in Ukraine while wartime-election politics roil Kyiv; Israeli strikes in Gaza undermine the ceasefire track Kushner just left; and the US carrier pull from the Pacific is deepening allied fears of a strategic retreat in Asia. The through-line is a US stretched across multiple fronts, escalating economically in the Gulf while its naval and diplomatic commitments elsewhere come under strain.

item.title: Strategic Brief: US Sanctions ICC President Tomoko Akane as Washington Escalates Court Campaign, Seoul Cuts Drills by Half
item.description:
The Trump administration sanctioned the International Criminal Court's president and a senior trial lawyer, deepening its campaign against the Hague-based court, while the US and South Korea slashed their annual joint exercise at Trump's direction and Gaza's restricted areas expanded to nearly two-thirds of the territory.
► US Sanctions ICC Leadership in Escalating Court Campaign Secretary of State Marco Rubio announced sanctions on Tuesday against ICC President Tomoko Akane of Japan and senior trial lawyer Abdoulaye Seye of Senegal, according to the US Treasury Department and Middle East Eye. Why it matters: Sanctioning the sitting ICC president is a direct escalation of Washington's effort to dismantle a court that has pursued cases against US allies and non-member states, signaling that the administration will not tolerate ICC jurisdiction over American personnel or partners.
► US and South Korea Cut Ulchi Freedom Shield by Nearly Half South Korea and the United States agreed to shorten their annual Ulchi Freedom Shield exercise, ending it Friday instead of the originally scheduled August 27, at the request of President Trump, Yonhap reported. Why it matters: Halving the flagship US-South Korea exercise and dropping its counter-attack phase is a concrete concession to Pyongyang that weakens the allies' demonstrated deterrent posture, even as North Korea denounced the drills.
► Gaza Restricted Areas Expand to 64.9 Percent Since Ceasefire Since the Gaza ceasefire took effect on October 10, 2025, Israeli military operations have continued, more than 1,200 Palestinians have been killed and restricted areas have expanded to 64. Why it matters: The expansion of restricted areas to nearly two-thirds of Gaza shows the ceasefire has become a vehicle for consolidating Israeli control rather than a step toward a political settlement, with the second phase of the agreement effectively frozen.
► Ghana Reports 62 Citizens Killed in Ukraine War as Minister Presses Moscow Ghana's Foreign Affairs Minister Samuel Okudzeto Ablakwa said 62 Ghanaians have been killed and 15 remain missing in Russia's war against Ukraine, disclosing the figures during bilateral talks with Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov in Moscow, pe Why it matters: The confirmed deaths of 62 Ghanaian citizens in the Ukraine war underscores the scale of foreign recruitment into the conflict and gives African states a direct stake in pressing Moscow over the treatment of their nationals.
► Hormuz Standoff Deepens as Trump Labels Strait 'New US Territory' President Trump posted a map on Truth Social labeling the Strait of Hormuz as 'NEW U. S. Territory,' drawing a circle that also takes in a portion of mainland Iranian territory on the northern shore, per MercoPress. Why it matters: With the ceasefire MoU expired and no formal talks scheduled, Trump's territorial claim and the naval blockade keep the world's most critical oil chokepoint shut and the risk of renewed conflict high.
■ The Bottom Line Washington escalated its campaign against the International Criminal Court by sanctioning its sitting president, a first, while simultaneously cutting the US-South Korea exercise nearly in half at Trump's direction — two moves that signal a more aggressive posture toward international institutions and a more conciliatory one toward Pyongyang. In Gaza, restricted areas have grown to 64.9 percent of the territory since the ceasefire, showing the truce has hardened rather than reversed Israeli control. Ghana's disclosure that 62 of its citizens have been killed in Ukraine highlights the war's widening human toll, while the expired US-Iran ceasefire and Trump's claim over Hormuz leave the world's key oil chokepoint shut and the risk of renewed conflict high.

item.title: Strategic Brief: US Expands Anti-Cartel Campaign to Land in Latin America as Iran-Oman Hormuz Deal Nears and 60-Day Deadline Expires
item.description:
The Pentagon is moving its Western Hemisphere counter-cartel campaign from sea to land after killing hundreds in boat strikes, while Iran and Oman finalize a shipping-management plan for Hormuz just as the US-Iran negotiating window lapses without an extension.
► US Anti-Cartel Campaign Shifts From Sea to Land in Latin America AP reports that the US military is expanding its counter-cartel operations in Latin America from the sea to the land, after a campaign of boat strikes that has killed hundreds. Why it matters: A US land campaign against cartels in Latin America carries far higher risk of direct confrontation with sovereign governments and civilian casualties than maritime interdiction, and signals a permanent US military footprint in the region.
► Hormuz: Iran and Oman Finalize Shipping Plan as US Deadline Expires AP reports that Iran says it is working to finalize a joint statement with Oman on a plan to manage shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, where oil tankers and container vessels were seen at a standstill on Monday. Why it matters: The expiry of the 60-day window without an extension removes a formal deadline that had structured diplomacy, while an Iran-Oman shipping plan could either be the basis for reopening Hormuz or a way for Tehran to control the strait on its own terms.
► Ukraine Targets Russia's Economy and Morale Through Online Retailer AP reports that Ukraine is delivering blows to Russia's economy and morale by attacking the online retailer Wildberries, including a drone strike on a warehouse in St. Petersburg in late July. Why it matters: Attacking a mass-market retailer is a different kind of warfare than hitting military infrastructure — it is designed to erode public tolerance for the war inside Russia, where the Kremlin has tried to insulate ordinary citizens from its costs.
► Iran War's Ripple Effects Threaten Education for Millions of Children AP reports that the ripple effects of the Iran war could threaten education for millions of children around the world, hitting the poorest first. Why it matters: The war's humanitarian cost is not confined to the Middle East; its economic fallout is quietly eroding education access for the world's most vulnerable children, a long-term consequence that will outlast the fighting.
► Brazil's Lula Backs Amazon-Mouth Drilling After Petrobras Find AP reports that Brazil's President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva said on Monday that oil drilling in northern and northeastern coastal regions could be 'a passport to the country's future,' after visiting a Petrobras offshore vessel following a hydrocarb Why it matters: The discovery gives Lula a potent economic argument heading into a close election, but it pits Brazil's development ambitions against its climate leadership and the environmental concerns of the Amazon region.
■ The Bottom Line The day's defining moves were expansions and deadlines: the US pushed its counter-cartel campaign onto land in Latin America, Iran and Oman moved toward a shipping-management deal for Hormuz just as the 60-day US-Iran negotiating window lapsed without extension, and Ukraine broadened its war on Russia's economy by striking a mass-market retailer. Brazil's Amazon-mouth oil find added a major energy-development story, while the Iran war's economic fallout continued to reach classrooms in Southeast Asia. The common thread is a widening of fronts — geographic, economic and diplomatic — rather than any single decisive breakthrough.

item.title: Strategic Brief: Trump Cuts US-South Korea Drills After Seoul Declines Iran Role, Kushner Meets Hamas on Gaza Road Map
item.description:
Washington signals it will 'substantially reduce' joint exercises on the peninsula days before Ulchi Freedom Shield, linking the move to Seoul's refusal to join US operations against Iran. Separately, Jared Kushner held a rare meeting with Hamas leadership in Egypt to salvage the stalled Gaza disarmament plan.
► Washington Downgrades the Korea Alliance President Donald Trump said the United States will 'substantially reduce' joint military exercises with South Korea, citing his 'very good relationship' with North Korean leader Kim Jong Un and Seoul's refusal to take part in what he called the 'denu Why it matters: This ties the future of the US-South Korea alliance directly to Seoul's willingness to back Washington's Iran war, and hands North Korea a diplomatic opening — potentially reviving Trump-Kim talks while loosening the military pressure that has underpinned the peninsula's deterrence.
► Kushner Sits Down With Hamas as Gaza Plan Teeters US envoy Jared Kushner met Hamas's new political chief, Khalil al-Hayya, in Egypt on Sunday — the first meeting at that level since last year's ceasefire — in a push to salvage the US-backed 15-point Gaza road map, according to the BBC and AP. Why it matters: Washington is now negotiating directly with the group Israel refuses to recognize, and eight regional powers are publicly siding against Netanyahu. That isolates Israel ahead of its October 27 election and tests whether Trump can override a key ally on the core issue of Hamas disarmament.
► Ukraine Launches Largest Drone Attack of 2026 Russia said at least seven people were killed in what officials called the 'largest-scale' attack Ukraine has launched this year — around 822 drones, with 600 aimed at Moscow, whose regional governor called it 'one of the most massive drone attacks i Why it matters: The exchange shows the war has become a long-range attrition contest over logistics and missile stockpiles. Ukraine's reliance on home-built drones is being tested precisely as US Patriot supplies dry up, and both sides are betting on the other exhausting its capacity to strike first.
► Iran Standoff Nears a Deadline Al Jazeera's live coverage flagged that the Tehran-US memorandum of understanding is set to expire on Monday, with the terms of that expiry still unclear. Why it matters: The expiring MoU is a concrete near-term trigger for escalation or de-escalation. Combined with Washington's evident frustration over allied contributions, the Iran file is now driving changes in US posture far beyond the Middle East itself.
► Ebola in DR Congo Becomes the Country's Deadliest Outbreak The Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo has killed 2,325 people, surpassing the toll of the 2018-2020 outbreak to become the deadliest in the country's history, Al Jazeera reported, citing the DRC's National Public Health Institute Why it matters: A rising death rate — not falling — signals the response is losing ground. With no approved vaccine for this strain and conflict disrupting access, the outbreak threatens to become a regional humanitarian emergency, not just a Congolese one.
► Zambia's Incumbent Leads as Opposition Alleges Armed Raid Zambian President Hakainde Hichilema held nearly 59 percent of the vote with more than half of constituencies counted on Sunday, putting him on course for an outright first-round victory, Al Jazeera reported, citing the electoral commission. Why it matters: Zambia has transferred power peacefully through elections since 1991, making the armed-raid allegation a significant test of that record. A disputed result would carry weight across a region watching whether African elections can still deliver credible outcomes.

item.title: Strategic Brief: Indonesia Quake Kills 47 as Trump Vows to Declare Hormuz US Territory, China-Philippines Clash in South China Sea
item.description:
A magnitude 7.7 earthquake struck Indonesia's Flores region, killing at least 47, while President Trump said he will 'soon' declare the Strait of Hormuz a US territory and a new China-Philippines clash injured a Filipino sailor at a disputed shoal.
► Magnitude 7.7 Quake Hits Indonesia's Flores Region A magnitude 7. 7 earthquake struck off Indonesia's coast early Saturday, killing at least 47 people and toppling buildings, according to the US Geological Survey and the Indonesian National Search and Rescue Agency (BASARNAS). Why it matters: A major humanitarian disaster in a region already strained by years of natural disasters; the shallow quake's coastal location raises the risk of landslides and a possible tsunami threat, and the toll is likely to climb.
► Trump Says He Will Declare Hormuz a US Territory President Donald Trump said he will 'soon' declare the Strait of Hormuz a US territory, according to Al Jazeera, which noted that the comments overstate the level of US control over the international shipping route. Why it matters: A unilateral US territorial claim over an international strait would be a major legal and diplomatic rupture, and the carrier redeployment leaves the western Pacific without a US carrier just as China shows more assertiveness in the region.
► China-Philippines Clash at Second Thomas Shoal The Philippine military accused China's coast guard of injuring a Filipino sailor during an incident at the disputed Second Thomas Shoal in the South China Sea, AP reports. Why it matters: The South China Sea incident and Taiwan's budget approval both come as the US carrier absence from the Pacific raises questions about Washington's ability to reassure allies in the region.
► Israeli Strikes Kill 11 in Southern Lebanon Israeli air strikes killed at least 11 people and wounded 19 in southern Lebanon, according to the Lebanese Ministry of Health, as attacks intensified across several towns overnight. Why it matters: The strikes threaten to unravel the fragile ceasefire and the US-mediated border talks that Lebanon had described as making 'positive progress' just over a week ago, and Hezbollah's rejection of direct negotiations signals a hardening of positions.
► Erdogan Says Egypt Could Join Turkey-Saudi-Pakistan Defence Pact Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan said Egypt could join the joint defence agreement recently signed by Turkey, Saudi Arabia and Pakistan, describing Cairo's accession as 'possible' and the pact as open to further members, in an exclusive intervi Why it matters: Expanding the Mecca Pact to include Egypt would significantly broaden a new Middle East security bloc at a time when the US-Iran war and Hormuz closure are reshaping regional alignments.
► Ukraine Strikes Russian Satellite-Internet Network Ukraine used domestically produced Flamingo cruise missiles to strike targets in Russia's southwestern Samara region, hitting a military airfield and a rocket centre that supports Russia's Starlink-style satellite internet network, according to Al Ja Why it matters: Ukraine's long-range strikes deep into Russia, including against satellite-communications infrastructure, show Kyiv's growing domestic strike capability even as Moscow presses Washington and Ankara over a potential transfer of US-held weapons from Turkey.
■ The Bottom Line A magnitude 7.7 earthquake killed at least 47 in Indonesia's Flores region, while President Trump escalated the Iran conflict by vowing to declare the Strait of Hormuz a US territory and pulled the last US carrier out of the Pacific. In Asia, a new China-Philippines clash at Second Thomas Shoal and Taiwan's passage of a $93 billion defence budget underscored the region's unease over the US focus shifting away from the Pacific. item.title: Strategic Brief: Farage Wins Clacton as Watchdog Probe Resumes, Trump Orders Navy Back to Steam Catapults, US Calls West Bank Settlers 'Terrorists'
item.description:
Reform UK's Nigel Farage returns to Parliament but faces a revived ethics investigation; the White House orders a costly rollback of the Navy's electromagnetic catapults; and Washington issues an unusually sharp rebuke of Israeli settler violence in the West Bank.
► Farage Back in Parliament, but the Watchdog Is Waiting Reform UK leader Nigel Farage won the Clacton on Sea by-election on Friday, returning to the House of Commons after abruptly quitting his seat in July. Why it matters: Farage is seen by some as a possible next prime minister, but the revived ethics probe keeps a legal sword hanging over his return — a reminder that his political trajectory now runs through a compliance process, not just the ballot box.
► Trump Orders the Navy Back to Steam Catapults President Donald Trump issued a directive Thursday ordering the Navy to remove the Electromagnetic Aircraft Launch System (EMALS) from its newest Ford-class carriers and return to older steam catapults, according to AP. Why it matters: A costly, ideologically driven rollback of proven technology at a moment of acute naval strain — and a widening gap with China and France on carrier design — raises questions about US naval readiness precisely when carriers are being surged toward the Middle East.
► Washington Calls West Bank Settlers 'Terrorists' For five nights, Israeli settlers surrounded three Palestinian homes in the occupied West Bank village of Qusra, including one owned by a Palestinian American. Why it matters: The public break between Washington and settler groups is notable given Trump's pro-settlement record, and it signals the administration is willing to police the West Bank's most volatile flashpoints even as it backs Israel elsewhere.
► Two UAE Tankers Hit by Drones in the Strait of Hormuz Two UAE tankers were attacked by drones while transiting the Strait of Hormuz, AP reports, the latest incident in the ongoing wartime campaign against vessels and infrastructure in and around the waterway. Why it matters: Drone attacks on commercial tankers in Hormuz keep the world's most critical oil chokepoint in a state of active hazard, sustaining the risk premium on global energy even as diplomatic efforts to reopen the strait continue.
► Kushner Heads to Israel and Egypt to Push Gaza Deal Jared Kushner will travel to the Middle East next week to try to advance plans to end the Gaza conflict, AP reports, after a Trump administration deal for Hamas to disarm ran into Israeli opposition. Why it matters: The high-level visit is a test of whether the US-brokered disarmament framework can survive the gap between Hamas's acceptance and Israel's insistence on full disarmament before any withdrawal.
■ The Bottom Line Today's developments are less about a single dramatic shift than about the machinery of several ongoing crises. Farage's return to Parliament is shadowed by a revived ethics probe; Trump's catapult order injects cost and risk into a Navy already stretched thin; and Washington's sharp rebuke of West Bank settlers marks a notable departure from its usual posture. Meanwhile, drone attacks on tankers in Hormuz and a strike on Yemen's Mokha port keep the Gulf's shipping lanes in active danger, even as Kushner's trip to Israel and Egypt tests whether the Gaza disarmament deal can be revived. The through-line: several fragile arrangements — political, military, and diplomatic — are being stress-tested at once, and none has yet resolved.
